riskFactors.title: Tobacco Use
riskFactors.description: Responsible for ~25% of cancer deaths; leading preventable cause.

riskFactors.title: Obesity
riskFactors.description: Linked to 13+ cancer types including breast, colorectal, and liver.

riskFactors.title: Infections
riskFactors.description: HPV, HBV, HCV, H. pylori cause ~13% of cancers globally.

riskFactors.title: Alcohol
riskFactors.description: Increases risk for oral, liver, breast, and colorectal cancers.

riskFactors.title: Physical Inactivity
riskFactors.description: Associated with colorectal, breast, and endometrial cancers.

riskFactors.title: Air Pollution
riskFactors.description: Outdoor air pollution linked to lung cancer incidence.

riskFactors.title: UV & Solar Radiation
riskFactors.description: Sun exposure and artificial UV drive melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers.

riskFactors.title: Processed & Red Meat
riskFactors.description: High intake of processed meats increases colorectal cancer risk by 18%.

didYouKnow: Lung cancer remains the most diagnosed cancer globally with 2.6 million new cases in 2024.
Asia accounts for 49.2% of global cancer cases but 56.1% of cancer deaths.
Female breast cancer is the most diagnosed cancer in women with 2.3 million new cases.
By 2050, cancer cases are projected to reach 34.4 million — a 67% increase from 2024.

faq.q: How many new cancer cases occur worldwide each year?
faq.a: GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates approximately 20.6 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, equivalent to roughly 1 in 5 people developing cancer during their lifetime.

faq.q: What is the most common cancer globally?
faq.a: Lung cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer (12.8% of all cases), followed by female breast cancer (11.8%) and colorectal cancer (9.9%).

faq.q: How many people die from cancer each year?
faq.a: An estimated 9.8 million people died from cancer in 2024 — approximately 26,800 deaths per day.

faq.q: Which region has the highest cancer burden?
faq.a: Asia bears the largest share with 49.2% of global cases and 56.1% of deaths, reflecting both population size and late-stage diagnosis patterns.
